blocks.text: …being able to react calmly
Basic idea and goal 🐕
Street routines help us in our daily movement in urban areas, so that we can be out and about with the dog in a relaxed way and avoid unpleasant situations.
Street routines are trained practically in passing in everyday life once the basic routines are in place, and are then a relaxed routine performance in use.
Street routines help our dog to feel increasingly safe in encounter situations in the urban environment, because it learns that every encounter ends with a clear, familiar sequence.
Prerequisites: Basic routines such as “down” and “sit” as well as the TEAM WALK should already be well trained. Street routines build directly on these skills and complement them in everyday use.

Street routines help us in our daily movement in urban areas, so that we can be out and about with the dog in a relaxed way and avoid unpleasant situations. They are trained practically in passing in everyday life once the basic routines are in place, and are then a relaxed routine performance in use.
Street routines help our dog to feel increasingly safe in encounter situations in the urban environment, because it learns that every encounter ends with a clear, familiar sequence.
Prerequisites: Basic routines such as “down” and “sit” as well as the TEAM WALK should already be well trained. Street routines build directly on these skills and complement them in everyday use.
The route – sharpening perception 👁️
We walk our route in a relaxed way and sharpen our perception for situations that lend themselves to training the street routines.
Suitable types of encounter are: pedestrians, joggers, cyclists and other low-risk encounters of everyday life.

In doing so, we walk as trained in the TEAM WALK, in an upright, relaxed posture. The leash is always at a neutral length and is neither too short nor taut. Our posture is loose. In this way, our posture already tells the dog before every encounter: everything is fine here.
Basic sequence 🐾
Street routines are very easy to train with the appropriate attentiveness. We use every kind of distraction for our training.

As soon as our dog responds visually or acoustically to an approaching distraction, we walk, completely relaxed, to the nearest edge of the street or path and put the dog into “down”. In adverse conditions, “sit” is also acceptable.

We begin the training sequence at the earliest possible moment – that is, when the dog first notices the distraction – and end the sequence with warm praise once the situation has been fully completed.

The number of training repetitions is important : we should use almost every distraction situation that arises for this sequence. Over time we notice that our dog disengages from the distraction and performs the exercise more and more easily – precisely because it becomes routine.

After several weeks of use, we can move on to no longer treating every encounter this way. We then simply continue walking normally, knowing that we have trained an interruption tool that can be used at any time.
Posture and leash handling 🦮

Our posture is the first signal our dog reads in every situation. An upright, loose posture signals calm – tension, hunched shoulders or staring rigidly at the source of the distraction are immediately registered by the dog and interpreted as a warning signal.

The leash stays at a neutral length in every phase of the encounter. An abrupt shortening of the leash as a distraction approaches acts on the dog like a confirmation: now it is getting dangerous. We consciously avoid this reflex.

When guiding the dog into “down”, we move calmly and fluidly without jerking or pulling. The direction of movement towards the edge of the path is enough as a signal – over time our dog learns to take this route itself.

In the TEAM WALK the rule is: the transition into “down” when a stimulus appears happens seamlessly out of the walking movement. Once the situation is over, we resume the TEAM WALK just as calmly – without haste, without comment.
Progression levels – from easy to demanding 📈

Level 1 – Single pedestrians at a wide distance: The classic introduction. Quiet encounters on wide pavements or in parks with sufficient room to move aside. Here we consolidate the basic sequence and build trust.

Level 2 – Joggers and cyclists: Fast-moving stimuli require an earlier reaction from the dog handler. We take care to recognise the situation even further in advance and to position the dog in good time – before the stimulus is too close.

Level 3 – Several encounters in quick succession: Busy pavements, markets or school routes offer dense sequences of stimuli. Here we train the dog’s resilience and our own calm under sustained load. Short breaks and moments of relief between the repetitions are important.

Level 4 – Combination with further stimuli: Traffic noise, prams, skaters or unpredictable movements combined. This level is only tackled once Levels 1–3 are secure. It corresponds to the everyday level of a stimulus-rich city environment.
In general: Always train at the level at which our dog can still work safely and without being overwhelmed. Progress comes from repetition at the appropriate level – not from escalation.
Dealing with setbacks 🔄

Setbacks are a normal part of any training and not a sign of failure. If our dog reacts much more strongly than usual on a given day, this is often a signal of increased baseline tension – for example due to lack of sleep, preceding stimuli or health factors.
In such moments we deliberately step back to an easier progression level. We specifically seek out quieter streets, greater distances and lower stimulus frequency – instead of forcing the situation.

No praise for incomplete execution or while the arousal phase is still ongoing. We wait patiently until the dog has really settled. Praising too early confirms the state of arousal and weakens the routine in the long term.
After a difficult training day, we deliberately end the session with an easy, successfully completed situation – so that the dog (and we) finish with a positive experience.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid stressful and confusing situations for these training sequences at all costs.
Avoid confined situations in which moving aside or calm positioning is not possible.
Avoid situations of frontal confrontation.
Avoid situations that cannot be controlled as they develop.
Avoid abruptly shortening the leash as a distraction approaches – this creates counter-pressure in the dog and increases arousal.
Avoid training at a progression level that is above your dog’s current safe level – being overwhelmed costs more time than patient repetition.
Practical impulse: Routine beats reaction

The most effective moment is the earliest one. If you calmly lead your dog to the edge of the path at the very first glance towards the distraction, the exercise is half won. Do not wait until it pulls – act before it decides. The more often you do this, the more natural it becomes for it.
→ Does my dog reliably master “down” and “sit”?
→ Am I already training the TEAM WALK as a basis?
→ Do I recognise distraction situations early enough to react in good time?
→ Is my posture relaxed and upright – even when stimuli approach?
→ Do I keep the leash neutral – without abrupt shortening or pulling ahead?
→ Do I use almost every encounter situation as a training repetition?
→ Am I training at a progression level that allows my dog to experience success?
→ Do I only praise after the situation has been completed fully and calmly?
→ In the case of setbacks, do I deliberately go back to an easier level instead of escalating?
→ Do I end every session on a positive note – for my dog and for me!
